newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia to maintain prudent fiscal policy.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia to maintain prudent fiscal policy.

text.p: Central bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono said on Wednesday the Indonesian government would maintain a prudent fiscal and monetary policy to keep domestic demand in check.
"Given the outlook of continued strong domestic demand, we must remain vigilant of upward pressures on prices," he told bank leaders at an industry dinner.
"For this reason, the government will maintain a prudent fiscal and monetary policy so as to keep domestic demand in check," he said.
Djiwandono said the government would continue to address supply bottlenecks by expanding domestic production through investment and expediting production and distribution.
"These measures are expected to contribute to a lower level of inflation in 1997 than in 1996," he said.
Indonesia's economy is projected to grow by about 7.8 percent in 1996 against 8.2 percent in 1995, with inflation seen at 6.47 percent in 1996, against 8.64 percent in 1995.

"Our economic fundamentals are definitely strong, but neither can we rule out the possibility of even strong shocks and we must all remain vigilant," Djiwandono said. Indonesia's currency weakened when President Suharto underwent medical checks in Germany in July 1996 after which he was given a clean bill of health.

The domestic financial market had also been rattled during a series of demonstrations staged by a rebel group in the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) after their leader Megawati Sukarnoputri was deposed as PDI leader.
"We are fortunate that none of these have produced major disturbances in the economy," Djiwandono said.
He said the country needed to stay alert for other market disruptions brought on by speculation related to non-economic issues such as the general election in May.
He said economic disruption, which could be caused by enormous short-term capital inflows, would quickly spread to other countries.
"Indonesia, Thailand, Hong Kong and Malaysia have experienced this contagion effect in the wake of the Mexican crisis," he said.
Djiwandono also said Indonesia's monetary policy in 1997 would continue to focus on strengthening macro-economic stability.
"For this purpose, credit growth is set at 17 percent in 1997/98 (April-March) and and this is expected to hold M2 growth down to 18 percent," he said.

Indonesia's 1997/98 state budget projects broad M-2 money supply to grow by 18 percent to 323.6 trillion rupiah in fiscal 1997/98, while narrow M-1 money was expected to rise by 16 percent to 71.55 trillion rupiah.
The year-on-year M-2 growth last November was 28 percent and M-1 was 19 percent.
